title: Christian Nationalism: A Five-Session Bible Study
subtitle: A pastoral five-session study on what Christian nationalism is and isn't, for people on every side of it, that keeps the cross above the flag.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult classes, and anyone tired of a phrase that gets thrown like a rock in two directions and wants to know what it actually names. It works through five of my essays. It defines Christian nationalism without slandering the man whose grandfather landed at Normandy, and it confronts the fusion of nation and faith without sneering at ordinary believers who love their country. A busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

It isn't a study that flatters one party and scolds the other. It asks the conservative whether he has married his country to God and won't let anyone question the marriage. It asks the progressive whether he fears religion in public only when it's the wrong religion, and whether he has put his own hope in the state. And it asks the same of me. I'm not writing from outside this temptation, and neither is anyone who leads it.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: What It Is and What It Is Not
sessions.aim: To define Christian nationalism carefully, as the fusion of nation and faith into one loyalty that can't be questioned, and to tell it apart from ordinary love of country.
sessions.summary:
Plenty of believers hear the phrase Christian nationalism as an insult to a grandfather who landed at Normandy. That's rarely what careful people mean by it. The phrase has been ruined in two directions: some use it as a slur against any patriotic faith, and others use it as a catchall for people they disagree with who happen to pray. Between those two, the real thing has nearly disappeared.

So I want to make the best case for the person who fears the phrase. Loving your country isn't a sin. God told the exiles to "seek the welfare of the city" where they lived (Jeremiah 29:7). But the sociologists Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry describe Christian nationalism as a cultural framework that fuses Christianity with American civic life, and the word that matters there is fuses. Patriotism loves a country and can still repent of its sins. The fused faith has made the nation something no one is allowed to judge. And the covenant many people assume is ancient is younger than it feels: "under God" entered the Pledge in 1954, and "In God We Trust" became the national motto in 1956.

keyScripture.why: "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting" (John 18:36). Jesus doesn't deny to Pilate that he's a king. He denies that his kingdom is the kind that comes from here or advances by this world's means.

discussion.q: When you first heard the phrase Christian nationalism, what did you assume it meant? Where did that assumption come from?
discussion.behind: Get both distortions into the open before defining anything. Some will hear an attack on patriots, others a label for the other side. You're not settling it yet, only showing that everyone arrived with a loaded definition, which is a good place for humility to start.

discussion.q: What's the difference between loving your country and worshiping it? Can you think of a real situation where your country and your Christ might ask different things of you?
discussion.behind: Push for something concrete. If no one can name a case, that's worth noticing. When faith and nation have been fused, the conflict never seems to come up, because the two have been arranged so they always agree.

discussion.q: "Under God" was added to the Pledge in 1954 and "In God We Trust" became the motto in 1956. What does it do to the idea of an ancient covenant to learn those dates?
discussion.behind: Loosen the assumption without mocking anyone. The point isn't that the people who said those words were insincere. It's that something can feel eternal and still have a birthday. Let people sit with that rather than rescuing them from it.

discussion.q: Whitehead and Perry found that Christian nationalism doesn't track with church attendance, prayer, or Bible reading, and on several questions it pulls the opposite way. What does that suggest about what Christian nationalism actually is?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. It suggests the fusion is less a deep faith than an identity, a way of marking who belongs to the nation in religious language. It can thrive in a life with very little of Jesus in it. Listen for that recognition. Some scholars dispute how the book measures religion, so hold the finding firmly but not as the last word.

discussion.q: Where do you feel the pull to want your country to be the kingdom, or to want your side to be?
discussion.behind: Move from definition to self-examination. Go first. You aren't after a confession that shames anyone, only the admission that this pull is in all of us, because nobody repents of something they're still calling a virtue.

objections.objection: This whole study is a way for the left to sneer at conservative Christians who love their country and their flag.
objections.response: Start with what's true in that. Throwing the phrase carelessly at faithful people who feed the hungry and bury the poor is its own sin, and I won't defend it. Plenty of people use "Christian nationalist" to end a conversation rather than to understand anyone. But this study isn't against loving your country. It's against a particular fusion, one where the nation can no longer be corrected because it has been joined to God. You can honor the grandfather at Normandy and still ask whether something he never would have recognized has crept into the faith of his grandchildren. That question isn't an insult to him.

objections.objection: Warnings about religion in public life are selective. People only fear faith in public when it's the wrong faith. A faith pushed out of public life just makes room for another establishment that pretends to be neutral.
objections.response: There's a lot of truth here. Lesslie Newbigin argued that there's no neutral public square. The question is never whether some faith shapes public life, but which faith and how. A secularism that thinks of itself as neutral is often another establishment in disguise. But that's an argument against false neutrality, not an argument for fusion. The answer to a hidden establishment isn't to install our own. It's a public faith that brings its convictions into the open and can still be corrected.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is one thing you love about your country that you would never want to lose?
sessions.practice: This week, notice one moment when you feel a stronger reaction to an insult against your country than to an insult against Christ. Don't try to fix it. Just notice how hot it ran, and write down what it told you.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we love our country, and that love isn't the sin. The sin is letting it grow so large that it can't be corrected. Show us the line at our feet that we keep crossing without noticing. Keep the cross above the flag in us this week, and give us the humility to hear the truth about what we've made ultimate. In the name of the King whose kingdom is not of this world, amen.
reflection: Where did I first learn to fuse my faith and my country? Did anyone teach it on purpose, or was it simply in the air?
What would it cost me to admit that my country could be wrong about something I care about?
If Christ and my country asked different things of me tomorrow, do I know which I would obey?
sessions.teaching:
Let's start where many believers start. They hear the phrase Christian nationalism as an insult to a grandfather who landed at Normandy, an accusation against everyone who ever put a hand over their heart for the flag. Usually that isn't what careful people mean. But they're right to be wary, so we'll be careful too. I want to say what this thing isn't before I say what it is, because the phrase has been ruined in two directions at once. To some it's a slur against ordinary patriotic faith. To others it's a lazy label that means little more than people I disagree with who pray. Between those two distortions the real thing has nearly vanished, and you can't resist something you can't name.

I want to make the strongest case for the person who fears the phrase, because it's a real case. Loving your country isn't a sin. When Israel was carried off to Babylon, God told them to build houses, plant gardens, and "seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare" (Jeremiah 29:7). If exiles were told to love Babylon, a Christian may surely love the country that raised him. Gratitude for its freedoms, its soldiers, and its harvests honors gifts that come from God. And the people who throw the phrase around have often never set foot in that man's church or watched his people feed the hungry and bury the poor. He's right about all of that, and the carelessness of his accusers is a sin of its own.

But everything he's describing is patriotism, and patriotism isn't what the phrase names. Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry, the sociologists who've done the most careful work on it, describe Christian nationalism as a cultural framework that fuses Christianity with American civic life: its myths, symbols, and sense of who belongs. The word carrying the weight is fuses. Patriotism loves a country. The fused faith joins the country to God and then won't let anyone pull them apart. Once they're joined, the nation can't be corrected, because correcting it would feel like correcting God.

So the test isn't whether you sing the anthem or honor the dead. The test is what happens when your country and your Christ ask different things of you. A patriot grieves and obeys Christ. The fused faith has quietly arranged its theology so the conflict never comes up. Jesus put the difference plainly when he stood before Pilate, the man who held Rome's power in that room: "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world" (John 18:36). He didn't deny being a king. He denied that his kingdom comes from here or runs on this world's fuel. The proof he gave was that his followers weren't fighting.

It helps to know, too, that the covenant many people assume is ancient isn't. The Pledge of Allegiance was written in 1892 without the words "under God," which Congress added in 1954. "In God We Trust" became the national motto in 1956. Both changes came during the Cold War, when America wanted to mark itself off from an officially atheist enemy. That doesn't make the people who said those words insincere. It does mean that something can feel eternal and still have a birthday.

One finding should give every believer pause. In Taking America Back for God, Whitehead and Perry report that Christian nationalism doesn't rise and fall with church attendance, prayer, or Bible reading, and that on a number of questions it pulls the opposite way. Some critics dispute how they measure religion, and that's fair to say. But the pattern suggests the fusion is often less a deep faith than an identity, a way of marking who belongs to the nation in Christian language. It can flourish in a life with very little of Jesus in it.

I'm not standing outside this. Many of us received a faith that was already fused with the flag and didn't question it for years, and some of us who now see it clearly feel a different pull, to make our own side the righteous one. So we'll stand inside this together, and begin by learning to tell love from worship.

scriptureStudy.note: "My kingdom is not of this world." Jesus answers the man with the power to kill him. He doesn't deny that he's a king. He denies the kind of king Pilate fears.

"Of this world" translates a Greek phrase that means "out of" or "sourced from" the world. Jesus isn't saying his kingdom has nothing to do with this world. He's saying it doesn't come from here or run on this world's power.

"If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting." The proof is strange and decisive. A kingdom that fights to put its king on the throne is, by Jesus' own test, a kingdom of this world.
"Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf." Hold this beside John 18. Love of a place is commanded, even a place that isn't your own.
"They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them." When Israel wants a king like the nations, God names it as a change of throne.

"The God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people." God's kingdom is given, not seized, the opposite of a plan to capture the state.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, look at the history behind the founding story. Historians, Mark Noll among them, have shown that the founders ranged from devout Calvinists to skeptical deists, and that the story of a Christian founding lost and waiting to be reclaimed is more complicated than it sounds. In America's God, Noll also traces how nineteenth-century Americans learned to read God's favor directly off national events, which he treats as a theological error and not only as bad history.

Underneath that, notice that Christian nationalism can work like a rival story of salvation, with the nation as the vehicle of redemption: its founding a covenant, its decline a fall, its restoration something faithful citizens must accomplish. Once you see that shape, you can ask whether Jesus is at the center of it or only decorating it. A group with theological training might compare Augustine's two cities with the two-kingdoms tradition of Luther and later Reformed thought, and ask where each protects the church from fusion and where each can be misused to excuse doing nothing. And test Whitehead and Perry fairly. Their measures come from survey questions, so ask what those questions capture and what they miss. The goal is to learn the data's limits, not to use it as a weapon.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a retired Army veteran in your group has said little all evening. When you reach the question about the dates, he finally speaks. His father flew bombing runs over Germany. When you put 1954 and 1956 next to the Pledge and the motto, he says, it feels like you're calling his father's faith a fad that Congress invented, and he isn't sure he can keep coming if that's where this is headed. He isn't angry. He's hurt, and the room goes quiet because everyone respects him.

Can you honor him fully, saying plainly that his father's faith was real and his service was real, and still let the dates stand as dates? The point was never that his father was a fraud. It's that an arrangement can feel eternal and still have a birthday, and learning the birthday doesn't insult the people who lived inside it. Sit with him. Don't rush to rescue the room from the discomfort.

memoryVerse.text: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world."

devotional.title: An Insult Never Spoken
devotional.body:
Paul tells the Romans to welcome the one who is weak in faith, "but not to quarrel over opinions" (Romans 14:1). Before you decide what you think about Christian nationalism, notice how easy it is to hear an attack where only a question was asked. Someone names a fault in something we love and we feel the heat rise before we've understood the words.

That heat tells you something. It shows where your loves are tangled, where you've fastened something to your own worth so tightly that a fair question feels like an assault. The exiles in Babylon had every reason to despise the city that held them, and God told them to seek its welfare and pray for it. That's a love that can survive the truth about its city. Ask God today for a love of your country sturdy enough to hear it questioned without flinching, and humble enough to learn something from the person asking.
devotional.prayer: Father, show me where I've tied my worth to something that can be questioned. Give me a love steady enough to hear hard words without hearing an enemy. Make me slow to take offense and quick to understand.

devotional.title: Two Distortions
devotional.body:
"The one who states his case first seems right, until the other comes and examines him" (Proverbs 18:17). The phrase Christian nationalism has been ruined in two directions, and both are sins of the tongue. Some use it as a slur to dismiss faithful people without listening to them. Others hear a slur no matter how carefully it's meant.

Most of our arguments about this are people stating their case first and loudly and never letting anyone examine it. Today, resist the reflex to define the person across from you by the worst version of what they believe. Recovering the careful meaning of a word takes patience, the patience to say what a thing isn't before saying what it is. That patience is a form of love. Ask yourself whether you've been more interested in being right about this than in being truthful.
devotional.prayer: Lord, guard my tongue from the easy slur and my ears from false offense. Teach me to understand before I answer. Let me want the truth more than the win.

devotional.title: The Word That Carries the Weight
devotional.body:
"No one can serve two masters" (Matthew 6:24). We usually hear that about money and miss how well it fits nations. The word that matters in this study is fuses. Patriotism loves a country and can still repent of its sins. The fused faith joins the country to God so tightly that the two can't be told apart, and something you can't tell apart from God, you can't correct.

The problem is rarely that we consciously choose our country over Christ. It's the quiet welding that makes us assume they always want the same thing, so the choice never has to be made out loud. That's more dangerous than open idolatry, because open idolatry at least knows it has two masters. Ask God today to show you one place where you've assumed your country and your Christ want the same thing, and give you the courage to test it.
devotional.prayer: Master, you've told me plainly that I can't serve two. Show me where I've joined what should stay separate, so I can see which one I'm really serving.

devotional.title: A Covenant With a Birthday
devotional.body:
"Under God" entered the Pledge in 1954, and "In God We Trust" became the motto in 1956. Many believers carry those phrases as proof of an ancient covenant, and they're younger than some people in our pews. That isn't an attack on the phrases. It's an invitation to be truthful about where our sense of a Christian founding comes from.

Moses warned Israel not to "say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth'" (Deuteronomy 8:17). The national version of that sin reads God's approval straight off our own history, as if we could be sure heaven was on our side. Scripture is far more careful. God called Assyria "the rod of my anger" (Isaiah 10:5) and then judged Assyria too. A nation can be used by God and still stand under his judgment. Today, hold your country's story a little more loosely. Thank God for its real gifts without claiming to know heaven's verdict on it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, keep me from reading my own favor into your providence. Let me thank you for real gifts without claiming a covenant you never made. Teach me a humbler love of country.

devotional.title: The Line at Your Feet
devotional.body:
"Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:12). Most of us cross the line from love into worship without ever seeing it. The danger isn't only for the obvious zealot. It's for the ordinary believer who is sure he'd never confuse the flag and the cross, and has stopped watching the line at his feet.

The test is simple. What happens in you when your country is wrong? Not in theory, where everyone admits it could be, but in the moment, when a specific failure is named and your throat tightens to defend rather than to grieve. End this week by asking God to make you someone whose love of country can still hear its country corrected, who grieves its sins instead of denying them, and who keeps the cross above the flag in the actual order of their loves.
devotional.prayer: Father, I think I stand, so guard me from the fall I can't see. Show me the line at my feet. Keep my love for my country small enough to be corrected and my worship of you whole. Amen.

sessions.title: Loving Versus Worshiping Your Country
sessions.aim: To draw the line between love, which can be corrected, and worship, which can't, and to ask which one we give our country.
sessions.summary:
Children sometimes ask, after a parade, why we put our hands over our hearts. We make nearly the same gesture in two places, before the flag and when we pray, and a child notices the rhyme an adult has stopped hearing. Love and worship aren't opposites. Worship is what love becomes when it stops admitting any limit.

So I want to defend the love before I warn against the worship, because the warning isn't fair without the defense. A Christian may love his country truly. But love can be corrected and worship can't, because correction assumes a standard above the thing, and worship has put the thing where no standard reaches it. The test isn't how you feel at the parade. It's what you do when your country is wrong. Augustine taught that sin is disordered love, a lesser good loved as if it were the greatest. The problem isn't the size of the love. It's where the love has been put.

keyScripture.why: "They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them" (1 Samuel 8:7). When Israel demands a king "like all the nations," God names it for what it is, a transfer of trust from the God they couldn't see to the strength they could.

discussion.q: We put a hand over the heart before the flag, and many of us fold our hands or bow when we pray. What do you make of the similarity?
discussion.behind: Let the image carry it. You aren't trying to prove the gesture is idolatry. You're helping people feel the rhyme a child would notice, so the rest of the session has somewhere to land.

discussion.q: What does someone who loves their country do when their country is wrong? What does someone who worships it do?
discussion.behind: Make the contrast clear. The lover says "my country" and grieves and resists. The worshiper says "my country" and defends it, because otherwise his god has failed. Listen for anyone who realizes they can't remember the last time they let their country be wrong.

discussion.q: Augustine said sin is disordered love, a good thing loved out of its proper place. Where does love of country sit in your own order of loves?
discussion.behind: This is the center of the session. A drunk doesn't simply love wine too much; he loves it above his health and his family. Help people see the question isn't how much they love their country but where that love sits next to Christ, the church, and the stranger.

discussion.q: Read 1 Samuel 8:4-20. Israel wanted a king to be "like all the nations." Where do you see that same trade today? Does it only run in one political direction?
discussion.behind: Keep this even on purpose. The longing for a strong Christian nation and the hope that the state will finally set the world right can be the same trade in different clothes. Don't let the room make it one party's sin.

discussion.q: What makes you angrier, an insult to the flag or an insult to Christ? What does your answer tell you?
discussion.behind: Close by turning the question inward. The thing we defend most fiercely often shows what we actually worship, whatever we confess on Sunday. Go first if the room is slow.

objections.objection: Every warning against nationalism cuts one way. Nobody scolds the rootless cosmopolitan who feels nothing for any place. Suspicion of patriotism is really contempt for ordinary people and their loyalties.
objections.response: That contempt is real and common, and it should be named. Someone who loves no place isn't holier than someone who loves a particular one, and rootlessness isn't a virtue. This study isn't an argument for a cold heart. It's about the difference between a warm heart and an enthroned country. Nobody is being asked to love their country less. The question is where that love sits.

objections.objection: Saying that wanting your country to be great is really rejecting God as king just baptizes passivity. It lets injustice run because Christians are too holy to want anything for their nation.
objections.response: That concern deserves the same care. Wanting good for your country isn't the sin. Israel was told to seek the welfare of Babylon. What God named in 1 Samuel 8 was a matter of trust, the moving of ultimate hope from the God they couldn't see to the strength they could point to. You can work hard for justice in your country and still refuse to make it your god. Those aren't in tension.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When was the last time you felt your throat tighten with love for a place or a people?
sessions.practice: This week, name one specific way your country has been wrong about something, say it out loud to one person, and notice whether your love survives saying it. If it does, that's the love God permits. If it can't, it may be closer to worship.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you alone belong at the top, where no standard stands above you, and we keep trying to put other things there. We've loved good gifts out of order and defended what we should have grieved. Put our loves back in order. Let us love our country with a love that can still tell it the truth, and let our worship belong to you, who were put to death by an empire and rose again. Amen.
reflection: What do I defend most fiercely, and what does that say about what I worship?
Can I name a time I've said out loud that my country was wrong?
Where in my life is a good love sitting in the wrong place, ruling what it should serve?
sessions.teaching:
Children sometimes ask, after a parade, why we put our hands over our hearts. The easy answer is respect for the country and for the dead. The truer answer is that we make nearly the same gesture in two places, before the flag and when we pray, and the rhyme between them is what this session is about. Underneath the child's question is one of the oldest questions a believer faces: what may I love, and how much, before love becomes worship?

Love and worship aren't opposites. Worship is what love becomes when it stops admitting any limit. And a country is one of the easiest things in the world to love past its limit, because it asks for that love openly, with music and graves and the names of the fallen, and holding anything back can feel like betraying the dead.

So I want to defend the love first, because the warning isn't fair without the defense. A Christian may love his country truly. The same Scripture that sent Israel into exile told them to seek Babylon's welfare and pray for it. The throat that tightens at a military funeral isn't sinning. That's love, and love is good, and the people who sneer at it have often never loved a place enough to be embarrassed by their own tears.

Now the line, drawn plainly. Love can be corrected. Worship can't. You can love your wife and still tell her she's wrong, still refuse to follow her into something evil, and the love survives the correction and may even deepen through it. But the thing you worship can't be corrected, because correction assumes a standard above it, and worship has put it at the top where no standard reaches. So the test of whether you love your country or worship it isn't how you feel at the parade. It's what you do when your country is wrong. The lover says "my country" and grieves and resists. The worshiper says "my country" and defends it, because otherwise his god would have failed.

Reinhold Niebuhr saw how this works. In Moral Man and Immoral Society he argued that patriotism takes the unselfishness of individuals and turns it into the selfishness of a nation, and that the nation's claim on unqualified devotion is what frees it to use its power without restraint. A good love pushed past its limit doesn't simply stay good on a larger scale. It starts to demand sacrifices and silence consciences. Augustine named the root much earlier. Sin is disordered love, a lesser good loved as though it were the greatest. A drunk doesn't simply love wine too much. He loves it out of order, above his health and his family and God. In the same way, the problem isn't that someone loves their country too much. It's that the love has been placed above the kingdom, above the stranger, and above the Christ who made the stranger in God's image. The problem was never the size of the love. It's the place the love was put.

Scripture's hardest text on this is 1 Samuel 8. The elders of Israel come to Samuel and say, "appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8:5). Samuel is hurt, and God answers him: "Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them" (1 Samuel 8:7). Then God has Samuel warn them what the king will cost. He'll take their sons for his chariots, their daughters for his kitchens, and the best of their fields. They answer, "we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles" (1 Samuel 8:20). Their wish to be like the nations wasn't only a political preference. It was a transfer of trust, away from the God they couldn't see and toward the strength they could point to.

That trade runs in more than one direction. One person longs for a strong Christian nation to fight his battles. Another trusts the state to bring the justice and peace only God can finally bring. And the line runs through me too. Many of us get hot at an insult to the flag and stay cool at an insult to the cross, and that difference in temperature tells the truth. What we defend most fiercely is often what we actually worship, whatever we confess on Sunday.

scriptureStudy.note: "Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations." The longing to look like the powers around them drives the whole request.
"Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you." God gives them what they ask, and the gift becomes their discipline.
"They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them." The sin is named as a change of king. The throne changed hands in their hearts before it changed in the nation.
God spells out the cost. The king will take their sons, their daughters, and the best of their fields. What you enthrone to save you will eventually take from you.
"That our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles." The people refuse to listen. Worshiped strength always promises to fight our battles, and it sends our children to do it.

"You shall have no other gods before me." The first commandment isn't only about statues. It's about the place something occupies, and a country can occupy that place while everyone insists they still worship God.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, follow Augustine's reasoning further. In On Christian Doctrine he distinguishes things to be enjoyed for their own sake from things to be used, that is, loved for the sake of something higher. He locates sin in enjoying what should be used and using what should be enjoyed. A nation belongs among the good things that are real and worth loving but are meant to be loved in reference to God, who alone is to be loved for his own sake. In that light, Christian nationalism isn't a matter of degree. It's enjoying a second thing as though it were first.

Set Augustine beside Niebuhr's The Irony of American History, where the danger is less the wicked nation than the virtuous one, whose real goodness tempts it to believe its power is innocent. Augustine places the disorder in the loves of the individual soul; Niebuhr warns that groups are even better than individuals at justifying themselves. Then read 1 Samuel 8 against the rest of the Bible. Israel's monarchy is both a judgment on their unbelief and the line through which David and finally Christ come. God works even through the king he warned against. That forbids the lazy reading that all national structure is simply faithless. The question isn't whether nations may exist. It's where trust finally rests.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a member of your group, a social worker with progressive convictions, has been nodding along all evening, comfortable that the study is aimed at the conservatives she argues with at family dinners. Then you reach the question about which way the trade runs. She says, almost in passing, that of course government should be the one to fix poverty and injustice, because that's what loving your neighbor looks like at scale.

Her concern for the poor is real and good, and you should say so plainly. Then ask the gentle question this session is built for: where does her hope finally rest? If the state is what she trusts to make the world right, she has made the same trade Israel made when it asked for a king like the nations, only her king wears different colors. The same is true of the conservative who trusts a strong Christian nation to save. Don't let the room aim this at only one side.

memoryVerse.text: And the LORD said to Samuel, "Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them."

devotional.title: Two Rooms, One Gesture
devotional.body:
We put a hand over the heart before the flag, and we fold our hands when we pray. A child notices the rhyme. The point isn't that honoring a country is wrong. It's that the body learns devotion through repetition, and similar postures in two places can quietly teach the heart that the two places hold the same kind of thing.

Jesus said, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind" (Matthew 22:37). That total claim leaves room for lesser loves beneath it, but not beside it. Today, pay attention to your own postures: what you stand for, what makes you put a hand to your chest, what stirs in you the feeling worship is meant to stir. Then ask whether those feelings are pointed in the right direction. The body is truthful. It will show you where your devotion is aimed if you watch it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you ask for all of me, and I've given pieces to lesser things and called it loyalty. Show me what shares your place in my heart.

devotional.title: Seek the Welfare of the City
devotional.body:
Before any warning, hear the permission. God told the exiles to "seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf" (Jeremiah 29:7). That wasn't grudging tolerance. It was a command to love a place that wasn't even theirs. If exiles were told to love Babylon, you may love the country that raised you and fed you and buried your father.

Rootlessness isn't a virtue. The person who feels nothing for any place isn't holier than the one whose throat tightens at a familiar hymn. So don't be afraid of your love for your home and your people. Let it be warm. Thank God for the particular place he set you, its rivers and roads and graves. The whole point of drawing a line between love and worship is to let love be what it is, sturdy and unashamed, without the weight of a devotion it was never meant to carry.
devotional.prayer: Father, thank you for the place you've set me, its gifts and its people and its graves. Let me love it freely and well, and never put it in your place.

devotional.title: Disordered Love
devotional.body:
Paul says the human race "exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25). Idolatry, for Paul, isn't mainly the love of evil things. It's created things put in the Creator's place, good gifts asked to be God. Augustine called it disordered love.

That's both a relief and a warning. A relief, because you don't have to stop loving your country to be faithful. A warning, because the disorder is subtle, a matter of where a love sits rather than whether it's present, and you can carry it for years without noticing. Today, take stock of your loves, and ask not how much you love each thing but where each one sits. What have you placed above what?
devotional.prayer: Lord, you're to be loved for your own sake, and everything else loved through you. Put my loves back in order. Lower what I've raised too high and lift what I've let fall.

devotional.title: A King Like the Nations
devotional.body:
"But the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel. And they said, 'No! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations'" (1 Samuel 8:19-20). God read the desire correctly. It wasn't a policy preference. It was a transfer of trust, away from the God they couldn't see and toward a strength they could point to. He gave them the king, and the king took exactly what Samuel said he would take.

The same trade still runs in more than one direction. The person who longs for a strong Christian nation to fight his battles and the person who trusts the state to bring a justice only God can bring may be making one trade in two costumes. Both want a visible strength to do what they no longer trust the invisible God to do. Today, look for the place where you've asked a human power to be your king. Name it plainly.
devotional.prayer: King of heaven, I've wanted a king I could see and a strength I could point to, and called that wisdom. Forgive the trade. Be my king again.

devotional.title: The Temperature Gauge
devotional.body:
The risen Christ says to the church in Ephesus, "I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first" (Revelation 2:4). They were busy, orthodox, and tireless, and their love had cooled. He measured them not by their activity but by the temperature of their love.

Measure yours the same way. What raises your temperature fastest? What insult lands hardest? Many of us run hot at an insult to the flag and cool at an insult to the cross, and that tells the truth about the order of our loves. It isn't a comfortable test. But Christ names a cooled love in order to call it home, not to condemn it. "Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first" (Revelation 2:5).
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, I've run hot for lesser things and cool toward you. Bring me back to my first love. Amen.

sessions.title: Flags in the Sanctuary
sessions.aim: To look at how worship spaces teach, and why a national symbol set beside the pulpit and the table can join two faiths together whether or not anyone meant it to.
sessions.summary:
Two flags stand on the platform of many American churches, and usually no one now in the building put them there. They appeared sometime in the last century, often without a vote. Moving them now would feel like aggression, though placing them felt like nothing. That difference is worth noticing. We'll defend an arrangement we never chose to make.

I want to make the best case for the flag first. It can express gratitude and honor members who served and didn't come home, and taking it down can be a sneer rather than a confession. A bare platform can serve pride as easily as a crowded one can serve idolatry. But the question I'd ask is about place. Not the lobby, where we might thank God for a free country, but the platform beside the pulpit, in the space set apart for the Word, the table, and baptism. Where something stands teaches. Robert Bellah showed that American civil religion has its own sacred symbols. Bring a sacred symbol of one faith into the holy space of another, and over time the two blur.

keyScripture.why: "The priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD" (1 Kings 8:11). The temple was built for one glory, and when that glory came, it filled the house.

discussion.q: Why do we often defend arrangements we never chose more fiercely than the ones we did?
discussion.behind: Start with the pattern, not the flags. Inherited arrangements shape us beneath the level of choice. Help people see it in their own lives before it becomes a debate about cloth.

discussion.q: Does it matter where a flag stands, the lobby or the platform? Why might the place change what it means?
discussion.behind: Keep the focus on placement, not presence. Something set beside the cross will in time be read as its equal. The eye learns from arrangement faster than the ear learns from speech.

discussion.q: Bellah described American civil religion as a real religion with its own sacred symbols and holy days. If he's right, what happens when a sacred symbol from one faith is set in the holy space of another?
discussion.behind: You're after the idea of fusion from session one. Worshipers can stop feeling any seam between the two and experience patriotism and faith as a single devotion.

discussion.q: Taking a flag down can be a sneer as easily as keeping it can be idolatry. How would you tell the difference?
discussion.behind: This keeps the study fair. The object isn't the disease; what it's allowed to mean is. Don't let the group conclude that a bare platform makes them holy. Pride can wear either arrangement.

discussion.q: Read 2 Kings 16:10-16. Ahaz didn't remove the Lord's altar; he moved it aside and gave its place to another. What have you grown used to in your own worship or home that might be doing the same thing?
discussion.behind: Turn it inward. Most of us let things stand because keeping them is easier than explaining them. Invite people to name their own second altar, which may not be a flag at all.

objections.objection: Taking the flag off the platform is just the church being ashamed of its country and siding with cultured people who look down on patriotic believers.
objections.response: Sometimes that's exactly what removal means, and it has been done as a sneer. That should be admitted plainly. The question isn't settled by moving cloth, because pride can strip a platform as easily as idolatry can drape one. What matters is what the symbol is allowed to mean. Begin by honoring the dead and the freedom to gather, and then ask the harder question about the space set apart for worship.

objections.objection: This is overthinking a piece of fabric. It's decoration. Reading idolatry into a flag stand is the kind of elite suspicion that alienates ordinary people in the pew.
objections.response: Contempt for ordinary believers is real, and the worry is fair. But the point isn't that cloth has power. It's that arrangement teaches without words, and a child raised beside two symbols of equal height takes in that equality long before he can name it. That isn't elite suspicion. It's paying attention to what a sanctuary teaches the children in it, whether or not anyone meant it to.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Think of the room where you first learned to worship. What stood at the front, and what did that teach you?
sessions.practice: This week, walk through your church or your home and read the room like a sermon. What stands in the place of honor, and what is it quietly teaching the children who grow up looking at it? Just notice, and bring what you saw to the next session.
sessions.closingPrayer: God of glory, you filled the temple until the priests could not stand, and you share your holy place with no rival. We've grown used to second altars and called them only cloth. Give us eyes to see the rooms we worship in. Where we've let a lesser glory stand beside the cross, give us the courage to pay the cost of moving it, and the humility to admit it when we haven't. Amen.
reflection: What stands in the place of honor where I worship, and what has it been teaching me without my noticing?
What have I grown used to that I would never have chosen?
What am I unwilling to examine because examining it would cost me with the people around me?
sessions.teaching:
There are two flags on the platform of many American churches, and the strange thing is that almost nobody chose them. The current pastor didn't put them there, and often neither did the one before. They appeared sometime in the last century, often without a vote, and they've stood beside the pulpit ever since with an authority no business meeting ever gave them. Moving them now would feel like aggression. Placing them felt like nothing. We'll fight to keep an arrangement we never chose to make, and something we'd fight to keep but would never have thought to install may have more power over us than the things we did decide.

I want to make the best case for the flag first, because the people who make it aren't fools. A flag in the sanctuary can be simple gratitude for a country that protects our freedom to gather. It can honor members who served and didn't come home, and removing it can wound the families of the dead for the sake of an idea. The church doesn't live in heaven yet. It lives in a particular country under particular laws, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of dishonesty.

The strongest version goes further. Removing the flag isn't neutral either. It can signal that the church is ashamed of its country, that it has joined the cultured people who look down on ordinary patriotic believers. Sometimes that's exactly what removal means. Flags have been taken down as a sneer rather than a confession. So the question isn't settled by moving the cloth. A bare platform can serve pride as easily as a crowded one can serve idolatry. The object isn't the disease. What the object is allowed to mean is.

So the question I'd ask is about place. Where does the flag stand? Not the lobby, where we might thank God for a free country, but the platform, beside the pulpit, in the space set apart for the Word, the table, and the water of baptism. Where something stands preaches every week, whether or not anyone notices, because the eye learns from arrangement faster than the ear learns from speech. A symbol that stands beside the cross will eventually be read as its equal, and a child raised in that room will absorb the equality long before he could put it into words.

Scripture treats sacred space as jealous space. When Solomon's temple was dedicated, "a cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD" (1 Kings 8:10-11). The house was built for one glory, and that glory filled it. And the Bible shows how things go wrong there. King Ahaz saw an altar in Damascus, had a copy built, and set it in the prime place before the temple, while the bronze altar that had stood "before the LORD" was moved aside to the north (2 Kings 16:14). He didn't remove the Lord's altar. He just gave its place to something else.

Robert Bellah, in his 1967 essay "Civil Religion in America," argued that the nation has a real civil religion of its own, with sacred symbols, holy days, and something like scripture. Bellah thought that civil religion could at its best call a nation to judgment, as Lincoln did. But if he's right that it's a religion, then carrying its most sacred symbol into the holy space of another faith isn't nothing. Over time worshipers stop feeling any seam between the two and experience patriotism and Christianity as a single devotion. That's the fusion we named in the first session.

Here's my confession underneath all this. In many churches the flags have outlasted every objection to them, and most of us pastors haven't been prophets clearing the temple. We've been the priest who got used to the second altar and told himself it was only cloth, because keeping it was easier than explaining it. Paul tells the church, "Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?" (1 Corinthians 3:16). So tonight we'll read our own rooms, not to feel superior, but to ask what they've been teaching us, and what stands in the center of our own hearts.

scriptureStudy.note: "A cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister." The glory itself crowded them out. The sanctuary is where one presence dwells and fills.
"For the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD." Not shared, not flanked, but filled. The space was built for one glory.
The second commandment forbids carved images and calls God "a jealous God." His jealousy isn't petty envy but the rightful, exclusive claim of a covenant Lord over his own house.
Ahaz moves "the bronze altar that was before the LORD" aside to make room for his new altar. He didn't remove the true altar. He gave its place to a rival.
Ezekiel sees "the image of jealousy" at the entrance of the inner court and hears that such abominations "drive me far from my sanctuary." A symbol in the wrong place does real spiritual harm.
"Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you?" The question of what stands in the holy place is now asked of the church and of each heart.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, read Bellah's essay on its own terms rather than as a slogan. He argued that American civil religion wasn't simply a corruption but a real and partly noble thing, able to call the nation to judgment as Lincoln did in his Second Inaugural. That sharpens the question. If civil religion can humble a nation as well as flatter it, what decides which it does? Can a national symbol placed in a sanctuary ever serve the humbling purpose, or does the placement itself remove the distance civil religion needs in order to judge?

Bring in the Bible's theology of sacred space too. The Old Testament's insistence on a jealous sanctuary isn't arbitrary ritual law. It's a long lesson in the exclusiveness of covenant worship, and the prophets saw other altars beside the Lord's as the way the house was lost. Notice that this session's worry isn't that material things are evil, but that arrangement shapes us, which is closer to the conviction that physical things form us than to a flat suspicion of images. Then face the hardest counterpoint. Cathedrals have long held the tombs and banners of a nation's dead. Was that always fusion, or are there ways of honoring the dead that don't enthrone the nation? Leave that question open.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a long-serving deacon, theologically conservative and deeply pro-life, tells the group he's become convinced that the two flags beside his church's pulpit are teaching his grandchildren something he never intended, and he wants to propose moving them to the fellowship hall. A younger member, also conservative, pushes back hard. He says this is exactly the surrender the culture wants, that once the church starts apologizing for the flag it has given in to people who hate it, and that the deacon is letting the left set the agenda inside his own sanctuary.

Both men love the same Lord and vote the same way. The younger man is right that removal can be a sneer and that the problem is in the meaning, not the cloth. The deacon is right that placement teaches and that children absorb it before they can name it. Don't settle it for them. Let the room see that two faithful conservatives can read the same platform differently, and that the real question is what the arrangement is allowed to mean.

memoryVerse.text: So that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD.

devotional.title: The Arrangement Nobody Chose
devotional.body:
The flags appeared without a vote, and now moving them would feel like aggression, though placing them felt like nothing. That's worth a week of attention, because it isn't really about flags. It's about how much of your life runs on arrangements you never chose and would now fight to keep.

Jeremiah says, "Stand by the roads, and look, and ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it" (Jeremiah 6:16). Standing by the road means stopping long enough to look at the path you're already on, the inherited one that feels like the weather. Much of what forms us was handed to us before we could weigh it. None of that is automatically wrong, and none of it is automatically right. Today, find one inherited habit in your life of faith and look at it. Not to tear it down, but to see it, and to ask whether you'd choose it now.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've inherited more than I've chosen, and I defend what I've never examined. Help me stop and look.

devotional.title: Where, Not Whether
devotional.body:
The question isn't whether a flag exists, but where it stands. When the temple was finished, "the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD" (1 Kings 8:11). The sanctuary was built for one glory. Where something stands teaches, because the eye learns from arrangement faster than the ear learns from speech.

This isn't only about church buildings. Your home has a place of honor too, a wall or a shelf or a screen that holds the center of your attention. Today, walk through the spaces where you live and read them like sermons. What occupies the central place? Whatever stands there is teaching you and the children who watch you, and the lesson is sinking in below the level of words.
devotional.prayer: God of glory, you fill your house and share it with no rival. Show me what I've put at the center of my home and my attention. Let one glory fill my life.

devotional.title: The Second Altar
devotional.body:
King Ahaz didn't tear down the Lord's altar. He moved it aside and put his new altar in the better spot (2 Kings 16:14). That's usually how it happens. Not a dramatic rejection of God, but a quiet reassignment of the best place, with the true altar still there, just nudged away from the center to make room for something that flatters more and asks less.

The danger of a second altar is that it doesn't feel like turning away from God. Everything still looks intact. The Lord's altar is there, just not where it was. Ask yourself the uncomfortable question today. Is there a second altar in your worship, something that has crept into the center while God's place moved to the side? It doesn't have to be a flag. It could be a cause, a comfort, or a fear. Look for what has the better spot.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've moved you to the side without meaning to and let something else take the center. Forgive me, and take your place again.

devotional.title: Jealous Space
devotional.body:
The second commandment calls God jealous: "You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God" (Exodus 20:5). We flinch at the word because we hear pettiness in it. But God's jealousy is the rightful claim of a covenant Lord over what is his. A husband who feels nothing when his wife gives herself to another doesn't love her more. He loves her less.

The sanctuary was built jealous on purpose, because the God who dwells there won't share the central place with other altars. That isn't insecurity. It's a love that refuses to be one option among several. Let that be a comfort today rather than a threat. He wants the whole of you, not a corner of you shared with a dozen lesser glories, and the God who refuses to share you is the God who will never let you go.
devotional.prayer: Jealous God, you won't share me, and I'm glad. Clear the rivals from the center of me, and be the one glory that fills my life.

devotional.title: The Priest Who Grew Used to It
devotional.body:
The risen Christ says to the church in Laodicea, "For you say, I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing, not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked" (Revelation 3:17). The most dangerous spiritual condition isn't open rebellion. It's the comfortable blindness of someone who has grown used to things and stopped seeing them.

In many churches the flags have outlasted every objection, and most of us aren't prophets clearing the temple. We're the priest who has grown used to the second altar and tells himself it's only cloth. Looking at what we've grown used to usually costs us something, often a disagreement with people who've grown used to it too. So end the week by asking where you've stopped seeing. The first step isn't to move anything. It's to stop pretending you don't see it.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, I've grown comfortable and called it peace. Open my eyes to what I've stopped seeing, and give me the courage to pay what seeing costs. Amen.

sessions.title: Whose Kingdom? Jesus and Political Power
sessions.aim: To see from the wilderness, Pilate's hall, and the cross that God's kingdom doesn't advance by seizing the means the world uses to win.
sessions.summary:
Before Jesus preached or healed anyone, the devil took him to a high place, showed him "all the kingdoms of the world and their glory," and offered them for a single act of worship (Matthew 4:8-9). Jesus refused. That refusal shapes his whole ministry. He wouldn't take the kingdoms of the world on the terms by which they're usually taken, and we reopen that question every election as if he hadn't settled it.

The strongest objection deserves a full hearing. The prophets confronted kings. William Wilberforce used political power to end the British slave trade, and Dietrich Bonhoeffer joined the conspiracy against Hitler. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people power crushes. All of that is true. The error isn't engagement. It's believing that engagement means seizing the throne, as if Christ couldn't reign unless his people ruled. The difference between Wilberforce and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup. And on the cross, Jesus took his throne by the one means no empire understands. He didn't seize power. He absorbed it.

keyScripture.why: "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me" (Matthew 4:9). The kingdoms are offered for one act of worship aimed the wrong way, and Jesus answers with the first commandment. Under the question of power, the real issue was always worship.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 4:8-10. Why does it matter that the offer of the kingdoms was a real temptation and not an empty one?
discussion.behind: If the temptation was hollow, it teaches nothing. In Luke the devil claims the kingdoms have been "delivered" to him (Luke 4:6). Real power is genuinely on offer to the church too, and the price is always a redirected worship that says power saves. Set this up as the pattern for the session.

discussion.q: How do you tell faithful public engagement from trying to seize the throne? What made Wilberforce different?
discussion.behind: This distinction keeps the study from sounding like a call to withdraw. Wilberforce pressed against a particular evil with the tools at hand and trusted a Lord who reigns whether or not the vote goes his way. He wasn't trying to make Britain the kingdom of God. Listen for the line between pressing a cause and installing a kingdom.

discussion.q: Jesus told Pilate that if his kingdom were of this world, his servants would be fighting. What does that do to the idea that God's kingdom advances by winning?
discussion.behind: A kingdom that fights to install its king is a kingdom of this world by Jesus' own test. Help people feel how much of our political imagination that rules out.

discussion.q: On Palm Sunday the crowd shouted "Hosanna," a cry for salvation, and many hoped for a king who would drive out Rome. Jesus came on a donkey. Where do we still want the king who conquers instead of the one who dies?
discussion.behind: Keep it even. On one side the hunger is for a Christian strongman; on the other, for a politics that will finally force the world right. Both want power that conquers. Don't let the room aim this at one side.

discussion.q: Think back to the last election night. Where did your hope go as the results came in?
discussion.behind: You're after where hope traveled, not how anyone voted. Go first if needed. The point isn't that caring about elections is wrong, only that our hope shows us which kingdom we're leaning on.

objections.objection: A kingdom not of this world is an excuse to retreat from politics and leave the vulnerable to whoever doesn't retreat. The prophets confronted kings. We should too.
objections.response: Almost all of that is right. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people power crushes, and a faith with nothing to say to Pharaoh isn't the faith of the Exodus. This study isn't a warning against engagement. It's a warning against the belief that engagement means seizing the throne. You can press hard against injustice and still refuse to believe that Christ needs Caesar's sword to finish his work.

objections.objection: If our side simply wins, righteousness advances and the country is saved. Voting the right way is the most important thing a faithful Christian can do.
objections.response: That's the wilderness offer again, this time in a voting booth: the belief that the kingdom is one majority away. The best answer is the cross. God's kingdom arrived through what looked like political defeat, when the power of the state was turned against the Son of God and couldn't keep him in the grave. A faith that needs to win has quietly admitted it no longer believes its own gospel can accomplish anything. Caring about an election isn't the sin. Putting your hope there is.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you could change one thing about the world by winning an election, what would it be, and would winning actually fix it?
sessions.practice: This week, whenever you feel the pull to believe a political victory would finally fix things, pray one line instead: "Your kingdom come, your will be done" (Matthew 6:10). Notice how it changes where your hope is resting.
sessions.closingPrayer: Jesus, you stood on a high place and refused the kingdoms of the world. You stood before Pilate and wouldn't let your servants fight. You took your throne by dying. We keep saying yes to the offer you refused and calling our yes obedience. Teach us the patience of a kingdom that doesn't need our majorities to arrive. Put our hope where it belongs, in the King who won by losing and can't be voted out. Amen.
reflection: Where did my hope go the last time the election results came in, and what does that show me?
Do I believe the gospel can do its work without political victory?
In my own life, have I been acting more like salt or more like someone planning a takeover?
sessions.teaching:
Before Jesus preached a sermon or healed a single person, he was taken up to a high place. "Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, 'All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me'" (Matthew 4:8-9). In Luke's telling the devil claims these kingdoms have been handed over to him (Luke 4:6). Whatever we make of that claim, Jesus treated the temptation as real. The price was one act of worship aimed the wrong way. And he refused: "Be gone, Satan! For it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve'" (Matthew 4:10).

That refusal shapes his whole ministry. He wouldn't take the kingdoms of the world on the terms by which they're usually taken. We reopen the question every election as though he hadn't settled it. We ask how the church should hold power and how it should bend the state toward righteousness, and those aren't foolish questions. But they come after an earlier one: does God's kingdom advance by the means the world uses? Jesus said no in the desert, said it again to Pilate, and said it loudest on the cross.

The strongest objection deserves a full hearing, because it isn't the objection of cowards. The prophets confronted kings. John the Baptist lost his head telling Herod the truth. Wilberforce spent decades in Parliament to end the British slave trade. Bonhoeffer joined the conspiracy against Hitler. A church that washes its hands of power has often washed its hands of the people that power crushes, and a faith with nothing to say to Pharaoh isn't the faith of the Exodus. All of that is true, and I don't want to grant only half of it.

The error isn't engagement. It's the belief that engagement means seizing the throne, that the kingdom is the kind you install by winning, as if Christ couldn't reign unless his people ruled. Wilberforce didn't try to make Britain the kingdom of God. He pressed against a particular evil with the tools he had and trusted a Lord who reigns whether or not the vote goes his way. Jesus called his people "the salt of the earth" (Matthew 5:13), and salt works from within. The difference between Wilberforce and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup.

Follow it to Pilate's hall. Standing before the one man in the room with the power to kill him, Jesus said, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting" (John 18:36). The proof he offered was that no one was fighting. A kingdom that fights to put its king on the throne is, by his own test, a kingdom of this world.

A few days earlier he'd ridden into Jerusalem. Zechariah had promised a king "humble and mounted on a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9), and the crowds shouted "Hosanna," a cry that means something like "save us." Many of them surely hoped he'd drive Rome out by force. He came on the animal of peace instead, and before the week was over a crowd in the same city was calling for his death, because he wouldn't be the king they wanted. They wanted power that conquers. He brought power that dies.

Most of us have wanted the shortcut too. I've felt the pull in election seasons to believe that if my side simply won, the kingdom would move forward, that righteousness was one majority away. That's the wilderness temptation in a voting booth, and it comes to the right and the left alike. Where our hope goes on election night tells the truth about which kingdom we're leaning on, and the truth doesn't always flatter us.

The cross settles it. There Jesus took the throne by the one means no empire understands. He didn't seize power. He absorbed it. He let temple and empire do their worst, prayed for his executioners, and on the third day God overturned their verdict. Paul says that God "disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him" (Colossians 2:15). That's how the kingdom comes. A church that grasps for political power hasn't understood the cross. It's trying to win a war that was already won by losing.

scriptureStudy.note: "The devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory." From high enough up, power always looks like the answer.
"All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." The price is a single bow. The bargain never admits how small the bow feels and how complete the surrender is.
"You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve." Jesus answers an offer of power with the first commandment. The issue was always worship.
"If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting." A kingdom known by its refusal of the sword is a different kind of kingdom at the root.
"Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey." The promised king comes on the animal of peace, not the warhorse.
"He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him." The throne is reached through the descent.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, set these scenes inside the New Testament's teaching about the powers. Read Colossians 2:15 and ask how a triumph won by being executed changes every theology of conquest. Then weigh three traditions against one another. The Anabaptist reading, voiced today by Stanley Hauerwas, says the church is itself a community with its own politics and that its first political act is simply to be the church. The two-kingdoms teaching of the magisterial Reformation distinguishes God's rule through the gospel from his rule through civil government. And the abolitionists show how much good Christians have done through public life. This study refuses both withdrawal and fusion; a careful group should ask exactly where that middle ground lies and whether it holds.

Keep the cross whole as you do. On the cross Christ defeats the powers and also bears our sin, and a political reading must not swallow the atonement until the cross becomes only an example. Finally, take up the hardest historical question. After Constantine, the church gained imperial favor, and in time built hospitals and schools and carried the faith through centuries. Was that simply a fall, or a mixed providence that also corrupted? My own sense is that the church too often traded a little faithfulness for a little power. But a serious group should ask whether every nearness to power is that trade, or whether faithfulness can live near a throne it doesn't worship.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose it's the week after a national election and your group meets on edge. A man who volunteered for the losing campaign says, with real grief, that he's afraid for the country and that he prayed for months for his side to win because he believed it was what God wanted. He's sincere, and he could belong to either party, because this happens in both directions every cycle.

The room will be tempted to comfort him by agreeing that the right side lost. Don't. The pastoral question isn't which side he was on. It's where his hope went, and what the depth of his fear shows about where it had been resting. Honor his grief, because caring about the country isn't the sin. Then ask gently whether a hope that a Tuesday in November could shatter was ever resting fully on the King who can't be voted out.

memoryVerse.text: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world."

devotional.title: The Real Offer
devotional.body:
"All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me" (Matthew 4:9). We sometimes soften the wilderness into a morality tale, but the temptation was real. Power was offered with no campaign and no war, for one bow.

That's how the temptation still comes to the church. The access is real, the seat at the table is real, and the price always seems modest: a small change in what we trust, a slight bow toward power as the thing that saves. The bow is never labeled worship. It's called wisdom, or effectiveness, or simply doing what works. Today, look honestly at the offers in front of you. Where is real power or influence available to you, and what small bow is quietly attached?
devotional.prayer: Lord, the offers are real and the price feels small, and that's the trap. Help me see the bow hidden in the bargain, and refuse it.

devotional.title: Salt or a Coup
devotional.body:
"You are the salt of the earth" (Matthew 5:13). Salt works by being scattered through something, preserving and flavoring it from within, not by taking over the kitchen. Wilberforce pressed against a particular evil with the tools he had and trusted a Lord who reigns whether or not the vote goes his way. He was salt.

A coup is different. It believes the kingdom must be installed by winning, that Christ can't reign until his people do. The question today isn't whether to engage. A faith with nothing to say to injustice has given up something it had no right to give up. The question is how. Are you scattered through your corner of the world as salt, working for good and trusting God with the outcome? Or have you staked the kingdom itself on whether your side controls the room?
devotional.prayer: Lord, make me salt and not a conqueror. Let me work for good with what I have and leave the outcome with you.

devotional.title: The Absence of Fighting
devotional.body:
"My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting" (John 18:36). Jesus offers Pilate a strange proof: the evidence for God's kingdom is the absence of the sword every earthly kingdom relies on.

That reaches further than literal violence. It touches the whole posture of grasping, the belief that Christ's cause depends on our taking control. Every time we're sure the kingdom advances only if we win, we've described a kingdom of this world. Today, look for the place where your faith has quietly picked up the sword, where you've decided the gospel needs you to seize something to keep it safe. Then put it down. Refusing to grasp isn't weakness. It shows which kingdom you belong to.
devotional.prayer: Jesus, you proved your kingdom by putting down the sword, and I keep reaching for it in your name. Teach me the strength of not grasping.

devotional.title: The King They Did Not Want
devotional.body:
"Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9). On Palm Sunday many in the crowd hoped for a king who would throw Rome out. The prophet had promised a king on the animal of peace. Before the week was over, a crowd in the same city was calling for his death, because he wouldn't be the king they wanted.

We still want the king who conquers rather than the one who dies, and the hunger runs in every direction. One side dreams of a strongman who will take the country back. Another dreams of a politics that will finally force the world right. Ask yourself today which king you've been cheering for. When you picture the world set right, do you picture the other side crushed, or a kingdom that comes the way Jesus came?
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've cheered for the king who conquers and turned from the one who dies. Teach me to want the King who came on a donkey.

devotional.title: Won by Losing
devotional.body:
Paul says God "disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him" (Colossians 2:15). The triumph happened through the execution. The powers thought they were winning and were being disarmed in the very act.

The church keeps forgetting this. We try to win a war that was already won by losing, grasping for a power Christ refused because we don't trust the victory he's already secured. So end the week with a plain question. Where did your hope go the last time the election results came in? If a Tuesday in November can shatter it, it wasn't fully resting on the King who won by dying and can't be voted out. Put your hope back where it belongs.
devotional.prayer: Lord Jesus, you triumphed where it looked like defeat, and I keep trying to win the war you already finished. Put my hope in your kingdom, and keep me faithful while it comes. Amen.

sessions.title: How the Religious Right Was Built
sessions.aim: To see that the political movement that taught a generation to equate faithfulness with voting was built by named people in years we can count, and so can be examined, and where needed, repented of.
sessions.summary:
Many younger Christians assume the religious right has always existed, that faithfulness has always come with a voter guide. But the movement they take for the weather is younger than many people in our pews. It's a particular coalition, built in the 1970s around particular concerns by organizers whose names we know.

I want to grant its strongest defense first. Christians weren't wrong to enter politics, the unborn are owed protection, and a faith with no public voice has given up something. But the history complicates the founding story. The usual account says the movement rose in response to Roe v. Wade in 1973. The historian Randall Balmer argues that white evangelical leaders were fairly quiet about abortion in the years right after Roe, and that what first mobilized many of them was the fight to keep tax exemptions for segregated Christian schools. That's a contested reading, and the cleanest version of it is too tidy for the evidence. What's fair to say is narrower and still uncomfortable: race was woven into the movement's beginnings more deeply than its own story admits. And anything built by people in years we can count can, by grace, be examined and rebuilt.

keyScripture.why: "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me" (Matthew 4:9). The same wilderness offer names the bargain the religious right was offered: real access and influence in exchange for a slow redirection of worship.
