discussion.behind: Something that hides the date it was built doesn't want you to know it could have been built differently. You're loosening the assumption that today's fusion of faith and party is simply what serious Christians have always been.

discussion.q: The unborn are owed protection, and a faith with no public voice has given up something. How do we hold those convictions while still examining the movement built around them?
discussion.behind: Keep this fair. Make sure people with strong pro-life convictions feel honored, not dismissed, before the harder history comes. The aim is to hold convictions as Christians, not as soldiers.

discussion.q: Balmer's argument that segregated schools, more than abortion, first mobilized evangelical leaders is disputed by other historians. Why is it important not to tell this story more cleanly than the evidence allows?
discussion.behind: Race and abortion were tangled together, not neatly one after the other. Model for the room how to hold a hard claim at its actual weight, and don't let anyone turn it into a weapon or a simple verdict.

discussion.q: In 1980 the new coalition rallied behind Ronald Reagan, a divorced actor, over Jimmy Carter, a born-again Sunday school teacher. What does that choice suggest?
discussion.behind: Let the room see that personal piety wasn't the deciding factor; political power was. Then notice that any tribe, left or right, can come to prefer a useful leader over a faithful one when it wants power badly enough.

discussion.q: Where were you handed something about faith and politics that you assumed was the ancient faith, and only later discovered had a date?
discussion.behind: This is the closing turn of the whole study. Most of us were handed a fusion and took it for the gospel. Nobody lied on purpose; people passed on what they'd been given. Go first, and keep the tone gentle.

objections.objection: This is just an attack on pro-life Christians, dragging up race to shame people who only ever wanted to protect the unborn.
objections.response: It isn't, and it shouldn't be used that way. The unborn are owed protection, and knowing this history doesn't require anyone to give up their convictions about justice or about unborn children. The segregation argument is contested, and this study presents it that way. The narrower point is only that race was woven into the movement's beginnings more deeply than its founding story admits. That's being truthful about where something came from, not attacking a cause. A conviction held as a Christian rather than as a soldier can survive learning its history.

objections.objection: Fine, the religious right was built, so the answer is for Christians to get out of politics entirely and stop imposing their faith on everyone.
objections.response: That's the opposite overcorrection. The error was never engagement. A faith with no public voice has given up something it had no right to give up. The point is to refuse the bow that comes with the kingdoms, to engage as Christians who can still be corrected rather than as a tribe organized only to win. Examining how a movement was built isn't the same as leaving the public square.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is one thing you were taught about faith and politics growing up that you've never stopped to examine?
sessions.practice: This week, trace one political conviction you hold back to where you first received it. Ask whether you hold it as a Christian or as a soldier, and whether you could still be corrected on it. Write down what you find.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, we were handed a building and told it was a revelation, and most of us never learned when it went up. Forgive us for the bows we made without noticing, and for the times we wanted the kingdoms more than the cross. Give us the freedom to examine what we were given without fear, to keep what is true, to repent of what was tribe dressed up as faith, and to follow you rather than a coalition. Amen.

When have I preferred a powerful person who served my side over a faithful one who didn't?
sessions.teaching:
Many younger Christians assume the religious right has always existed. They can't picture a time when American Christians weren't sorted into political camps, when faithfulness didn't come with a voter guide. To them it's the weather. But the movement they take for the air itself is younger than many people in our pews, built on purpose by people whose names we know, in years we can count.

That's the first thing to understand. The religious right isn't the ancient form of Christian political engagement. It's a particular coalition, built in the 1970s around particular concerns by particular organizers. Saying so doesn't make it evil. Coalitions get built for good reasons too. It only refuses the story the movement tends to tell about itself, that it's simply what serious Christians have always been. Something that hides the date it was built doesn't want you to know it could have been built differently.

The strongest defense deserves to come first, because there's truth in it. Christians weren't wrong to enter politics. The unborn are owed protection. A faith with no public voice has given up something it had no right to give up. Hold all of that.

But the history complicates the founding story. The usual account says the movement rose in response to Roe v. Wade in 1973. The historian Randall Balmer, who grew up inside evangelicalism, argues that this is largely a later explanation. He points out that in the years right after Roe many white evangelical leaders were fairly quiet about abortion. The Southern Baptist Convention had passed a resolution in 1971 supporting legal abortion in some circumstances, such as rape, incest, and danger to the mother's health. Balmer argues that what first mobilized many leaders was the government's move to deny tax exemptions to private Christian schools that discriminated by race, with Bob Jones University as the best-known case. Other historians push back. They point to Catholic opposition to abortion that came earlier and ran alongside, and to a slower evangelical awakening on abortion through the later 1970s. The clean story, segregation and not abortion, is too tidy for the evidence. What's fair to say is narrower and still uncomfortable: race was woven into the movement's beginnings far more deeply than its own story admits, whether or not it was the single spark.

The pieces came together quickly. Jerry Falwell founded the Moral Majority in 1979, gathering conservative Protestants, Catholics, and Mormons into a single voting bloc. In 1980 the coalition helped elect Ronald Reagan, a divorced Hollywood actor, over Jimmy Carter, a born-again Baptist who taught Sunday school. That choice says something. Personal piety wasn't the deciding factor. Political power was. And let's be clear that any movement, of any party, can come to prefer the useful leader to the faithful one once it wants power badly enough.

Scripture saw this bargain long before. In the wilderness the devil offered "all the kingdoms of the world and their glory" for one act of worship (Matthew 4:8-9). The kingdoms are real, and the price is a redirected worship. The religious right was offered real access and real influence, and the price was the slow reshaping of a faith around winning elections. Many people paid it without feeling it. Jesus asked, "For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" (Mark 8:36). It's fair to ask the same of a movement.

None of us can tell this story as outsiders. The movement formed many of us before we could examine it. For many, the first Christianity they received was already fused, faith and party joined so tightly that they assumed the joining was the gospel. Nobody lied on purpose. People handed on what they'd been handed. Knowing this history doesn't require anyone to abandon their convictions about justice or the unborn. It asks us to hold them as Christians rather than as soldiers, to refuse the bow that comes with the kingdoms, and to remember that we were handed something built, not something revealed. Anything built by people in years we can count can also, by grace, be examined and rebuilt. We start by learning when it went up.

scriptureStudy.note: Return once more to the wilderness offer: all the kingdoms for one bow. The bargain comes in every century, and the price never announces itself.
"You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve." The cure for the bargain isn't better politics but a worship so settled that access can't buy it.
"For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?" Ask it of a movement: what does it profit the church to gain a majority and lose the gospel?
"Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart." A coalition that prefers the useful leader to the faithful one has started looking the way the Lord refuses to look.
"Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength, whose heart turns away from the LORD." Trusting a coalition to save us is an old sin in new clothes.
"For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth." A faith organized for winning will eventually be tempted to work against the truth, and Paul says that road leads nowhere.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For a group that wants more, weigh the history fairly rather than choosing the version that flatters your side. Balmer made his case in a 2014 Politico essay and in his books. It leans heavily on the Bob Jones University tax-exemption fight and on Paul Weyrich's later account of what finally moved evangelicals to organize. Critics note the Southern Baptist Convention's mixed record on abortion in the 1970s and the earlier Catholic pro-life movement, and argue that the causes were braided rather than one after the other. Practice holding a contested claim at exactly its weight, neither waving away the uncomfortable racial history nor inflating it into a single tidy charge.

Daniel K. Williams's God's Own Party gives a well-documented account of how the coalition was assembled, and Mark Noll's The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind names the intellectual cost of trading careful thought for culture-war reflex. Then press the deeper question. If a movement was built around real moral concerns and also around grievance and racial defensiveness, how does the church repent of that history without throwing away the real goods tangled up in it? The 1980 election makes a good case study. Work through it slowly.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a lifelong Republican in your group, a man who has voted the same way for forty years and has led your church's pro-life ministry, hears the material on segregated schools and gets quiet, then firm. He says it feels like a setup, that people on the left have spent years trying to shame pro-life Christians by bringing up race, and that he resents a Bible study being used to make him apologize for caring about babies.

His hurt is real and his conviction is sincere. He's right that this history can be used as a weapon, and you should say so and mean it. But the history is contested, not invented, and this study presents it as contested. The point is narrow: race was woven into the movement's beginnings more deeply than its founding story admits, and learning that doesn't require him to give up a single conviction about the unborn. It only asks him to hold that conviction as a Christian rather than as a soldier. Don't let the room turn this into a verdict against him.

memoryVerse.text: For what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?

devotional.title: The Weather and the Building
devotional.body:
"You leave the commandment of God and hold to the tradition of men" (Mark 7:8). The sting of Jesus' rebuke was that the Pharisees could no longer tell the two apart. They'd received their traditions as if from heaven.

We do the same. Many younger Christians take the religious right for the weather, when it's a building younger than some people in our pews. We absorb a political fusion from the air of a church and assume it's the gospel, never asking when it was assembled or by whom. Today, take one conviction you hold about faith and public life and ask: is this the commandment of God, or a tradition of people that I received as if it were? You may keep it. But you should know which it is.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I've held human traditions as though they came from you, and I can't always tell them apart. Help me ask which is which.

devotional.title: The Things That Are True
devotional.body:
Before the hard history, hold the true things. "Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter" (Proverbs 24:11). The unborn are owed protection. A faith with no public voice has given up something it had no right to give up.

When we learn a hard history, the temptation is to throw out everything tangled up in it, including the good. Don't. The call is to hold your convictions about justice and the unborn as a Christian rather than as a soldier, which means holding them more deeply, not less, but with open hands instead of a clenched fist. Today, name one public conviction you hold because you believe it honors God and your neighbor. Thank God for it. Then ask whether you've been holding it as a Christian, ready to be corrected and refusing to hate, or as a soldier.
devotional.prayer: Father, you call me to speak for those who can't speak for themselves. Let me hold that call as a Christian and not a soldier, deeply and with open hands.

devotional.title: The Founding Myth
devotional.body:
"Take no part in the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead expose them" (Ephesians 5:11). The usual story says the religious right rose to defend the unborn. The fuller history says race was woven in more deeply than that story admits. It's contested, and we hold it at its actual weight. But a movement, like a person, can't repent of what it refuses to see.

The instinct to protect a founding story is strong, because the story is cleaner than the history and lets us feel pure. Today, practice that harder truthfulness on something close to home. Is there a story you tell about your family, your church, your country, or yourself that's cleaner than the evidence? Bring it into the light before God, who already knows the full version and loves you in it.
devotional.prayer: Lord, I edit my stories to be cleaner than the truth and call that peace. Show me what I've hidden, and let me face it in your light and mercy.

devotional.title: The Powerful Sinner
devotional.body:
"For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). In 1980 the new coalition rallied behind a divorced actor over a born-again Sunday school teacher. Personal piety wasn't what decided it. Political power was.

A tribe that wants power more than righteousness will always end up preferring the leader who delivers, and will learn to call that preference wisdom. That temptation belongs to no single party. Today, examine your own judgments. When have you excused in a leader from your side what you'd have condemned in one from the other side? That double standard shows where the cause has begun to take Christ's place. Ask God for one standard, applied to your own side first.
devotional.prayer: Lord, you look on the heart, and I look at who serves my side. Forgive my double standard, and give me one measure, starting with me.

devotional.title: Handed a Construction
devotional.body:
Paul reminds Timothy of "your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well" (2 Timothy 1:5). Faith comes to us through people who love us. And inheritances can carry treasure and rubble in the same box.

For many of us, the first Christianity we received was already fused with a party, and we assumed the fusion was the gospel. Nobody lied to us. We were handed what others had been handed. The work of a lifetime is to keep the treasure and set down the rubble without despising the hands that passed us both. End the week with gratitude and truthfulness together. Thank God for the people who gave you faith, even imperfectly, and ask for freedom to keep what's true and follow Christ rather than a coalition.
devotional.prayer: Father, thank you for the people who handed me faith, who loved me and also passed on things they'd never examined. Help me keep the treasure, set down the rubble, and follow Christ. Amen.

leaderPrimer:
Your table may seat a veteran and an activist on the same night: the man whose grandfather landed at Normandy and the woman who has spent a decade angry at what the church became. This study only works if you keep faith with both of them. The phrase Christian nationalism has been thrown in two directions, so some of your group will arrive braced to be called idolaters for loving their country, while others will arrive hoping, finally, to watch someone else get named. Disappoint them both. The moment the study lands on only one kind of person, it stops being about idolatry and becomes another political meeting, and you'll have taught the room that theology is just politics in a robe, which is exactly what these sessions refuse.

Draw the line where the essays draw it, between loving a country and worshiping one, and hold it in every direction. Honor the flag folded at a funeral. Grieve the flag draped over a cross. Lead from inside the temptation rather than above it, because that's the only place anyone can lead this from.

Expect the hard moments in session three, when the flags in the sanctuary stop being abstract, and in session five, when the history of the religious right comes close to home for people who were formed by it and loved by people inside it. Slow down there. Let the man defending his grandfather be heard, because he usually isn't defending nationalism at all. He's defending a grave. And keep Jesus in the wilderness in front of the room, offered every kingdom on earth for one bent knee, and refusing (Matthew 4:8-10). The kingdoms were never the problem. Worship was. Lead like a pastor at a graveside, not a commentator at a desk. If your group leaves loving its country more truly because it worships its country less, you'll have done something rare.

faq.q: Is this study just a way to attack conservatives who love their country?
faq.a: No. The first session says at length that loving your country isn't a sin, that Scripture told exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon, and that throwing the phrase around carelessly is its own sin. The target is never patriotism. It's a fusion that can't be corrected, a love that has grown too large to hear the truth. A conservative who loves his country, honors its soldiers, and keeps Christ above it has nothing to fear here. The study asks the same hard questions of the left, including whether progressives have put their hope in the state and whether they fear religion in public only when it's the wrong religion.

faq.q: Is this just a way for the left to baptize its own politics as the real gospel?
faq.a: It would be if it spared the left, and it doesn't. It names trust in government to bring salvation as the same trade Israel made when it asked for a king like the nations. It warns that taking a flag down can be a sneer as easily as keeping it can be idolatry. It treats the hunger for a politics that will finally force the world right as the same conquest dream it criticizes on the right. The gospel here isn't any party's program with a cross attached. If your politics comes through this study completely untouched, it's worth reading again.

faq.q: What's the actual difference between patriotism and Christian nationalism?
faq.a: Patriotism is love and care for a particular place and its people, and it can be criticized and corrected because it doesn't claim ultimate loyalty. Christian nationalism, as Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry describe it, is a cultural framework that fuses Christianity with American civic life. The word that matters is fuses. The test is what happens when your country and your Christ ask different things of you. A patriot grieves and obeys Christ. A fused faith has arranged things so the conflict never comes up. Love can be corrected. Worship can't.

faq.q: Aren't the founders proof that America was founded as a Christian nation?
faq.a: The record is more mixed than that. Historians, Mark Noll among them, have shown that the founders ranged from devout Calvinists to skeptical deists. The Constitution establishes no church, and the First Amendment forbids Congress to establish one. The phrases many treat as ancient are recent: "under God" was added to the Pledge in 1954 and "In God We Trust" became the national motto in 1956, both during the Cold War. None of this means faith played no part in the founding. It means the simple story of a Christian founding lost and waiting to be reclaimed is itself a later construction.

faq.q: Is the study saying Christians should withdraw from politics?
faq.a: No. Session four grants the whole case for engagement. The prophets confronted kings, Wilberforce worked to end the slave trade, and a church that washes its hands of power has often abandoned the people power crushes. The error the study names isn't engagement but the belief that engagement means seizing the throne. The difference between Wilberforce and Christian nationalism is the difference between salt and a coup. Withdrawal and fusion are both mistakes.

faq.q: If there's no neutral public square, isn't driving faith out just another establishment?
faq.a: Yes, and the study agrees, drawing on Lesslie Newbigin. The question is never whether some faith shapes public life, but which faith and how. A secularism that imagines itself neutral can be another establishment in disguise, and a believer who resents being told to leave his convictions at the door isn't wrong to resent it. But that's an argument against false neutrality, not for fusion. The answer to a hidden establishment isn't to install our own. It's a public faith that brings its convictions into the open and can still be corrected.

faq.q: Why bring up race when talking about the religious right? Isn't that shaming pro-life Christians?
faq.a: The study is careful here on purpose. It presents Randall Balmer's argument about segregated schools as contested, not settled, and refuses to use it to shame anyone. The unborn are owed protection, and knowing this history doesn't require anyone to give up a single conviction about justice or the unborn. The point is narrow: race was woven into the movement's beginnings more deeply than its own story admits. A conviction held as a Christian rather than a soldier can survive learning where a movement came from.

faq.q: Does "a kingdom not of this world" mean Jesus didn't care about justice here and now?
faq.a: No. When Jesus told Pilate his kingdom isn't of this world, the proof he offered was that his servants weren't fighting. He wasn't saying his kingdom has nothing to do with this world. He was saying it doesn't come from here and doesn't advance by this world's methods. The same Jesus announced good news to the poor and freedom for captives (Luke 4:18). Caring about justice isn't the error. Believing justice only comes when our side seizes the throne is.

faq.q: Is it really wrong to have a flag in a church sanctuary?
faq.a: The study deliberately doesn't make this a rule about cloth. It grants that a flag can express real gratitude and honor members who died in service, and that removing one can be a sneer as easily as keeping it can be idolatry. It asks about place and meaning: does it stand in the lobby or beside the pulpit, and what is it allowed to mean? A symbol set beside the Word and the table will in time be read as their equal, and children take that in before they can name it. The point isn't to rule on your church's furniture. It's to read the room you worship in and ask what it has been teaching.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't all of this just religion arguing about how to grab power?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study shares it. Its whole argument is that the faith of Jesus refuses to advance by seizing the state, that Jesus turned down the kingdoms of the world when they were offered, and that a Christianity that needs political victory has stopped believing its own gospel. If you've seen religion used as a tool for power, the study calls that a corruption, on the right and the left. What it offers instead is a faith whose founder took his throne by being executed and praying for his executioners. You don't have to accept that faith to see that this study argues against the very thing you distrust.

faq.q: If Christians don't try to make the laws Christian, won't the country just drift into immorality?
faq.a: The study doesn't counsel passivity, and it doesn't promise that refusing fusion makes a country righteous. Christians can work hard for justice and for good laws while refusing to make the nation their god. But a faith that can only hold a country by capturing its laws has a thin view of how God works. The early church changed the world around it without controlling any laws, by being a different kind of community. Laws matter. But a country isn't saved by its statutes, and a church that thinks it is has put its hope somewhere the gospel never put it.

faq.q: Does refusing Christian nationalism mean I have to vote a certain way?
faq.a: No. A study that told you how to vote would betray its own argument. Its concern is where your hope rests when the results come in, not which box you check. Two believers who have both refused the fusion can still vote differently in good conscience, weighing competing goods and reaching different judgments. The study asks you to hold your political convictions as a Christian rather than as a soldier, to refuse to hate the people across the aisle, and never to place in an election the hope that belongs to Christ.

faq.q: How do I lead this without a seminary degree or any training?
faq.a: The way it was built to be led, by a busy volunteer. Every discussion question carries a note for the leader, and every session ends in prayer. The teaching, the Scripture notes, and this leader's guide are there so you aren't improvising. The real qualification isn't training. It's a willingness to go first, to be truthful about your own heart, to keep the room safe for people who disagree, and to keep the study from turning into a fight. Read the leader's guide, settle your own heart, and trust the material.

timeline.event: The Edict of Milan, issued by Constantine and Licinius, grants toleration to Christians across the Roman Empire, beginning the long alignment of church and imperial power.
The Edict of Thessalonica under Theodosius makes Nicene Christianity the official religion of the empire.
Augustine completes The City of God, arguing that no earthly nation is the city of God and that two cities, formed by two loves, are mixed together in this age.

The Peace of Westphalia ends Europe's wars of religion and strengthens the modern state, confirming with changes the principle first set at Augsburg in 1555 that a ruler decides his territory's religion.
The United States Constitution takes effect, establishing no church; the First Amendment, ratified in 1791, forbids Congress to establish one.
Francis Bellamy writes the Pledge of Allegiance, without the words "under God."
The Scopes trial in Dayton, Tennessee, becomes a cultural defeat for fundamentalism and deepens its sense of a Christian civilization under siege.
Congress adds "under God" to the Pledge of Allegiance during the Cold War.
"In God We Trust" becomes the official national motto.
Robert Bellah publishes "Civil Religion in America," describing the beliefs and rituals through which the nation understands itself before God.
The Southern Baptist Convention passes a resolution supporting legal abortion in cases such as rape, incest, and danger to the mother's health.
The Supreme Court decides Roe v. Wade, which the religious right's founding story credits as its spark, though the record of the following years is more mixed.
Jerry Falwell founds the Moral Majority, gathering conservative Protestants, Catholics, and Mormons into a single voting bloc.
The new coalition helps elect Ronald Reagan, a divorced actor, over Jimmy Carter, a born-again Sunday school teacher.
Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry publish Taking America Back for God, a sociological study of Christian nationalism in the United States.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. Three things before we start. First, this study asks hard questions of every side, including yours and mine, so we're not here to score points against people who aren't in the room. Second, nobody has to perform certainty. You can be unsure out loud, and you can change your mind. Third, I'm in this too. I'm not leading from above it. Tonight we're looking at ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone speaks.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage and the essay say. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the week ahead, because none of this matters if it stays an idea.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop there, even though it isn't resolved, because some of this shouldn't be wrapped up neatly. Take it with you rather than leaving it at the door. Try the practice this week, and spend some time with the reflection questions on your own. Come back ready to be truthful, not finished. Let me pray for us before we go.

bibliography.title: Taking America Back for God: Christian Nationalism in the United States (2020)
bibliography.author: Andrew L. Whitehead and Samuel L. Perry
bibliography.note: A sociological study that describes Christian nationalism as a cultural framework fusing Christianity with American civic life, and measures it with national survey data. Background for session 1.

bibliography.title: Moral Man and Immoral Society (1932)
bibliography.author: Reinhold Niebuhr
bibliography.note: Niebuhr's argument that patriotism can turn individual unselfishness into national selfishness. Background for session 2.

bibliography.title: The Irony of American History (1952)
bibliography.author: Reinhold Niebuhr
bibliography.note: On the danger that a nation's real virtues tempt it to believe its power is innocent. Background for session 2.

bibliography.title: Civil Religion in America (1967)
bibliography.author: Robert N. Bellah
bibliography.note: The essay that describes American civil religion as a real religion with its own symbols and holy days. Background for session 3.

bibliography.title: America's God: From Jonathan Edwards to Abraham Lincoln (2002)
bibliography.author: Mark A. Noll
bibliography.note: Traces how American Christians came to read God's favor off national events. Background for session 1.

bibliography.title: Fundamentalism and American Culture (1980)
bibliography.author: George M. Marsden
bibliography.note: How fundamentalism came to see itself as defending a Christian civilization under siege, especially after the Scopes trial.

bibliography.title: Jesus and John Wayne (2020)
bibliography.author: Kristin Kobes Du Mez
bibliography.note: A history of how a militant picture of Christian manhood became tied to defense of the nation over the twentieth century. Readers who dispute her conclusions can still learn from her sources.

bibliography.title: The Gospel in a Pluralist Society (1989)
bibliography.author: Lesslie Newbigin
bibliography.note: Argues there is no neutral public square and that a gospel which only blesses a culture loses its power to call that culture to repentance. Used on both sides of session 1.

bibliography.title: After Christendom? (1991)
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas
bibliography.note: Insists that the church's first task is to be the church, not to run the country. One voice among several, not the study's settled position.

bibliography.title: Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony (1989)
bibliography.author: Stanley Hauerwas and William H. Willimon
bibliography.note: Known for the claim that the church doesn't have a social strategy, the church is a social strategy. Background for session 4, read alongside the study's support for public engagement.

bibliography.title: The City of God
bibliography.author: Augustine
bibliography.note: The two cities formed by two loves, mixed in this age, so that no earthly nation is the city of God. Background for sessions 1, 2, and 4.

bibliography.title: The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind (1994)
bibliography.author: Mark A. Noll
bibliography.note: Known for its opening claim that the scandal of the evangelical mind is that there isn't much of one. Background for session 5.

bibliography.title: God's Own Party: The Making of the Christian Right (2010)
bibliography.author: Daniel K. Williams
bibliography.note: A documented history of how the Christian right was assembled. Background for session 5.

bibliography.title: The Real Origins of the Religious Right (2014)
bibliography.author: Randall Balmer
bibliography.note: Balmer's Politico essay arguing that the fight over segregated Christian schools, more than abortion, first mobilized evangelical leaders. A contested reading; present it as one.

furtherReading: Confessions and On Christian Doctrine, Augustine, for a fuller account of disordered love behind session 2.
The Myth of a Christian Nation, Gregory Boyd, a pastor's accessible case against fusing God's kingdom with national power.
American Covenant: A History of Civil Religion from the Puritans to the Present, Philip Gorski, on how covenant language has both judged and flattered the nation.
Resident Aliens, Hauerwas and Willimon, for readers who want to press session 4's claim that the church is itself a kind of politics.
The Gospel in a Pluralist Society, Newbigin, for thinking harder about public faith without false neutrality or fusion.

glossary.definition: A cultural framework that fuses Christianity with national civic life and identity. As this study uses the term, it means a fusion that can't be questioned, not ordinary love of country.
Love and care for a particular place and its people. Unlike nationalism, it can be criticized and corrected, because it doesn't claim ultimate loyalty.

The shared beliefs and rituals through which a nation understands itself before God, such as appeals to God in inaugural addresses and the near-sacred status of founding documents. It can humble a nation or flatter it.
The long era in which church and state were bound together, and being a citizen and being a Christian were assumed to be the same thing.
The pattern, named for the emperor Constantine, of the church aligning itself with state power and pursuing its mission through the machinery of government rather than the way of the cross.
The teaching that God rules the world in two ways, through the gospel and the church, and through civil government, so the two shouldn't be collapsed into one.
Augustine's picture of the earthly city formed by love of self and the city of God formed by love of God, mixed together in this age so that no nation is wholly either.
God's gifts of order, beauty, and justice to all people and societies, believing or not, which let Christians honor what's good in their country without worshiping it.
The view that a modern nation's civil law should be governed directly by the laws of Old Testament Israel. One of the more extreme forms of wanting the state to enforce a faith.
God's governing of history. Scripture is much more careful than we are about reading God's approval straight off national events.
The capacity, learned from the biblical prophets, to name a nation's sins and call it to repentance from inside. A faith fused with the nation loses it.
Augustine's description of sin as love in the wrong order, a lesser good loved as though it were the greatest.
Treating something other than God as ultimate. The idol is usually a good thing that has been asked to be God, which is how a country can become one.
The political organization Jerry Falwell founded in 1979, which gathered conservative Protestants, Catholics, and Mormons into one voting bloc.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: The phrase Christian nationalism gets thrown in two directions, and few people using it stop to ask what it names. This five-session study looks carefully at what it is and isn't, and draws the line between loving your country and worshiping it. It asks hard questions of every side, including our own, and any volunteer can lead it without preparation. Join us as we learn to keep the cross above the flag.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on Christian nationalism, and before anyone tenses up, hear this: it isn't an attack on patriotism, and it isn't partisan. It asks hard questions of the right and the left, and of all of us. And it asks a simple, hard question: what happens when our country and our Christ ask different things of us? No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: Love your country. Refuse to worship it. The difference is whether you can still tell it the truth. A five-session study on what Christian nationalism is and isn't, for people on every side, that keeps the cross above the flag. Come as you are.
